Option record: {\"id\":\"Active-subspace reparameterization of the calibration\",\"title\":\"Reparameterize the calibration with active subspaces to shorten the MCMC chain\",\"summary\":\"Identify the few data-informed directions along which the forward model varies (the active subspace) and run MCMC only on those while sampling the prior elsewhere, the non-neural, interpretability-flavored cousin of feature extraction that directly attacks the autocorrelation time through reparameterization rather than hardware.\",\"root_link\":\"Bears on framer.md's conclusion that the real lever on long chains is reparameterization or better samplers rather than more cores, by supplying exactly such a reparameterization.\",\"compute_open\":\"More parallel compute buys gradient samples used to estimate the active subspace: published demonstrations stop at M=300 gradient samples recovering a dominant one-dimensional subspace (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1506.04190) and at a 100-dimensional forward model with a two-dimensional active subspace (https://doi.org/10.1137/15m1042127); what is unknown above that is whether a single linear subspace still captures RR posteriors carrying the artificial multimodality from cheap integrators (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1029/2009WR008648).\",\"sequential\":\"The chain is draw M gradient samples (two forward evaluations each by finite difference, or one adjoint pass) -> average the outer products into the active-subspace matrix -> eigendecompose -> run MCMC on the active variables only (~4 serial steps); the answer needs M gradient samples plus one MCMC chain, and one GR4J forward is so cheap that a single GPU stays nearly idle. The M gradient samples are mutually independent and only the active-variable MCMC must run serially, so the samples could run in parallel if the forward model were expensive enough to justify it; the nearest source that tried this is Constantine, Kent & Bui-Thanh's active-subspace-accelerated MCMC (https://doi.org/10.1137/15m1042127).\",\"source_urls\":[\"https://doi.org/10.1137/15m1042127\",\"https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1506.04190\",\"https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1029/2009WR008648\"]}. Root question: What limits Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models for river catchments, which needs long MCMC chains? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could that be fixed with a shit ton of GPU parallelism?. 1: # Are there mech-interp (Goodfire-style) solutions to the RR-calibration compute question?
2: 
3: ## Short answer
4: 
5: Goodfire-style mechanistic interpretability is a specific tool: train a sparse autoencoder (SAE) on a neural network's internal activations to recover a sparse dictionary of interpretable "features," then steer those features to test causal hypotheses (Goodfire, https://www.goodfire.com/research/understanding-and-steering-llama-3). The method is motivated by superposition — the hypothesis that networks pack more features than neurons into an overcomplete set of non-orthogonal directions, which SAEs are designed to disentangle (Cunningham et al. 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08600).
6: 
7: The framer's core question — whether long MCMC chains are limited by hardware or by posterior geometry — is not a question about a learned neural network. It is settled by the effective-sample-size definition of autocorrelation (Stan Reference Manual, https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html) and by the sampler-theory diagnosis that slow mixing "is frequently caused by an inappropriate selection of the proposal distribution" (Vrugt et al. 2009, https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-). A GR4J forward model and an MCMC proposal have no internal activations for an SAE to decompose and no feature for steering to move. So for the literal "does a shit ton of GPUs fix τ" question the honest answer is no — mech interp is the wrong tool.
8: 
9: But the framer's problem has two edges where Goodfire-style tools do apply: (a) the dominant modern rainfall-runoff model is now a learned neural network (an LSTM), and (b) the "geometry" behind long chains is exactly a "which directions actually matter" question, which is what features-plus-interventions are built to answer. Three concrete options follow.
10: 
11: ## SAE feature extraction on learned rainfall-runoff models
12: 
13: LSTM rainfall-runoff models already exist and are known to have interpretable internals: Kratzert et al. found that individual LSTM memory cells track snow accumulation/melt and soil-moisture states, and that the cell states behave as storages (https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/22/6005/2018/; https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.07903). Goodfire's method turns this from hand-inspection into an automated sparse dictionary: an SAE trained on the cell-state activations recovers monosemantic feature directions, which is what Cunningham et al. showed for language models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08600) and what King et al. have begun for geophysical MLPs, where SAEs reduced the average number of sensitive inputs per neuron by 33% and surfaced monosemantic features tied to temperature and fall-speed thresholds for precipitation phase (https://doi.org/10.1029/2025jh000769). The RR-specific payoff is to re-ask the framer's equifinality question at the feature level: which sparse features of the learned model are uniquely constrained by the runoff record, and which interchangeable feature sets reproduce it — a representation-level statement of Beven & Binley's equifinality (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305).
14: 
15: ## Feature steering to map the identifiable manifold
16: 
17: Goodfire's steering intervenes on a single SAE feature and observes the downstream change (https://www.goodfire.com/research/understanding-and-steering-llama-3); the SAE-V work generalizes this into controlled interventions that validate a feature's causal role (https://arxiv.org/html/2502.06755v1). Applied to a differentiable RR model — an LSTM, or GR4J with the automatic differentiation Krapu et al. used for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2021WR031377) — one could steer each feature and measure the change in simulated runoff or likelihood. The features that move the hydrograph are the directions the data identify; the features that do not are the equifinality directions that set τ. This is a causal map of the posterior geometry the framer identifies as the binding constraint (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2003WR002378), produced by intervention rather than by assuming a proposal.
18: 
19: ## Active-subspace reparameterization of the calibration
20: 
21: The mech-interp instinct — a few sparse directions carry all the information — has a non-neural cousin that already attacks MCMC directly: active subspaces identify the low-dimensional directions along which a forward model actually varies and separate "the low-dimensional subspace that is informed by the data" from "its orthogonal complement that is constrained by the prior" (Constantine, Kent & Bui-Thanh 2015, https://doi.org/10.1137/15m1042127). Running MCMC on the active variables while sampling the prior on the inactive ones is precisely the reparameterization the framer identifies as the real lever on long chains, and the subspace can be estimated from M gradient samples via finite differences at two forward evaluations each, regardless of input dimension (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1506.04190). The open question for RR specifically is whether a single linear subspace survives the artificial multimodality that cheap fixed-step integrators inject into the posterior (Schoups et al. 2010, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1029/2009WR008648).
22: 
23: ## What mech interp cannot touch
24: 
25: Structural and input (rainfall) error — the modeling/likelihood changes Renard et al. describe as altering the posterior — and the data-availability limit are not feature-decomposition problems (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2009WR008328). No SAE or steering intervention recovers parameters a record cannot identify.

1: # What actually limits Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models — and whether "a shit ton of GPUs" fixes it
2: 
3: ## 1. My understanding, relayed before answering
4: 
5: Rainfall-runoff (RR) models map precipitation (and potential evapotranspiration) onto streamflow at a catchment outlet. The workhorse class for calibration studies is the lumped conceptual model — GR4J is the canonical example, with exactly **four** calibrated parameters and a simple production-store + unit-hydrograph structure evaluated a few thousand arithmetic steps per decade of daily data (Perrin, Michel & Andréassian 2003, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022169403002257). Bayesian calibration treats parameters as random and uses Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample the posterior p(θ | data).
6: 
7: Two facts dominate this literature:
8: 
9: 1. **Equifinality** — many different parameter sets reproduce the observed hydrograph almost equally well, so the posterior is broad, correlated, and often multimodal rather than a tight Gaussian around a single optimum. Beven & Binley (1992) state it directly: "within the limitations of a given model structure and errors in boundary conditions and field observations, different sets of values may be equally likely as simulators of a catchment" (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305).
10: 2. **Peculiar response surfaces** — hydrological model parameters are "highly correlated and interdependent," which is precisely what makes naive samplers mix slowly; summarizing/exploring the posterior is the stated bottleneck that "hindered widespread use of Bayesian techniques in hydrology" (Marshall, Nott & Sharma 2004, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2003WR002378). MCMC inefficiency is "frequently caused by an inappropriate selection of the proposal distribution" — a geometric/algorithmic problem, not a hardware one (Vrugt et al. 2009, https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-).
11: 
12: MCMC samples are autocorrelated. The information content of a chain of length N is the effective sample size ESS = N / (1 + 2Σρ_k), where ρ_k are lag autocorrelations; slow mixing inflates the integrated autocorrelation time τ and forces long chains to reach any target ESS (Stan Reference Manual, https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html). The integrated autocorrelation time is defined as the number of correlated samples needed, on average, to produce one independent draw (LaplacesDemon IAT/ESS documentation, https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/LaplacesDemon/help/ESS.html). So "needs long MCMC chains" is a symptom of large τ — a statistical property — not directly a statement about hardware speed.
13: 
14: ## 2. Predictions (stated before checking)
15: 
16: - **P1:** For a single lumped conceptual catchment, one forward run is so cheap that the likelihood is effectively free; the binding constraint is τ (mixing), not FLOPs.
17: - **P2:** The "long chains" requirement is a property of posterior geometry (correlation/equifinality/multimodality) and, secondarily, of numerical implementation; it is reduced by better samplers/reparameterizations, not by more cores.
18: - **P3:** GPUs help only where the problem decomposes into independent units of work: many chains (ensemble MCMC), many particles (SMC), many catchments (large-sample), or many forward runs (GLUE / expensive models). They cannot shorten a *single* chain's autocorrelation.
19: - **P4:** There are genuinely compute-bound levels — expensive distributed/high-dimensional models and large-sample (CAMELS-scale) studies — where more parallel compute changes what is even attempted.
20: 
21: ## 3. Analysis
22: 
23: ### 3.1 Why chains are long: geometry and numerics, not throughput
24: 
25: The reason hydrology needed MCMC at all — and found it hard — is that the posterior of a conceptual RR model is difficult to summarize and explore because parameters are strongly correlated (Marshall et al. 2004, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2003WR002378). Equifinality formalizes this as "equal finality": many parameter pathways reproduce the observed runoff (Beven & Binley 1992, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305). The DREAM paper's motivating diagnosis is that slow mixing "is frequently caused by an inappropriate selection of the proposal distribution," and its remedy is a self-adaptive differential-evolution proposal that tunes scale and orientation during the search — i.e., a better *algorithm*, not more *hardware* (Vrugt et al. 2009, https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-).
26: 
27: Autocorrelation is the currency here: τ is set by the target's geometry and the sampler, and is invariant to how many parallel chains you run. Running more chains increases the number of samples per wall-clock second, but each chain still pays the same τ per independent draw. That is why "just add GPUs" is not, by itself, a fix for slow mixing — it changes throughput, not τ.
28: 
29: There is also a subtlety specific to hydrology: **cheap numerics corrupt MCMC**. First-order, explicit, fixed-step integration of water-balance dynamics makes the model "computationally cheap" (explicitly desirable for MCMC), but that cheapness introduces artificial bimodality in marginal posteriors and causes "slow convergence of the MCMC algorithm" plus unreliable Gelman–Rubin diagnostics (Schoups et al. 2010, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1029/2009WR008648). Here the fix is a better ODE integrator (adaptive-step, second-order, or operator splitting), again not more compute.
30: 
31: ### 3.2 The per-evaluation cost is not the binding constraint (lumped models)
32: 
33: GR4J has four parameters and a compact store/unit-hydrograph structure (Perrin et al. 2003, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022169403002257; INRAE webGR, https://webgr.inrae.fr/eng/tools/hydrological-models/daily-hydrological-model-gr4j). A multi-decade daily simulation is a few thousand arithmetic steps. Tellingly, the original GLUE paper could call its procedure "computationally intensive" only because it ran on a 1992 "local parallel processing computer" (Beven & Binley 1992, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305) — the same embarrassingly parallel random sampling is trivial on any modern machine. For this model class, the bottleneck is the number of *serial* MCMC iterations needed to overcome τ, not the cost of each iteration.
34: 
35: ### 3.3 What "a shit ton of GPU parallelism" actually buys
36: 
37: MCMC within a single chain is inherently sequential (each state conditions on the previous one), so the only exploitable parallelism is across independent units of work. That covers three regimes:
38: 
39: - **(a) Ensemble / differential-evolution MCMC.** DREAM "runs multiple different chains simultaneously for global exploration" (Vrugt et al. 2009, https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-). Jeremiah et al. note that parallel chains "with different starting points enable the sampler to simultaneously explore multiple regions of the parameter space, thereby improving the posterior coverage over that of a single chain" (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2010WR010217). GPUs/cloud make thousands of chains cheap, which helps multimodal coverage and yields cross-chain convergence diagnostics — a real, but bounded, improvement (it does not reduce τ).
40: 
41: - **(b) Expensive forward models.** For spatially distributed models with hundreds-to-thousands of parameters, the cost of the forward model dominates, and "high-performance computing"/distributed computing delivers a "spectacular performance improvement" for the MT-DREAM(ZS) sampler on problems up to 241 parameters (Laloy & Vrugt 2012, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2011wr010608). GPU-optimized large-basin models report ~20× CPU speedups for calibration and ~65× GPU speedups for simulations (Freitas et al. 2022, https://experts.illinois.edu/en/publications/performance-optimization-of-the-mgb-hydrological-model-for-multi-). At the SWAT end of the spectrum, calibration "could take days to complete, even on the finest standalone machines" (nhess 2012, https://nhess.copernicus.org/articles/12/2411/2012/nhess-12-2411-2012.pdf). This level is genuinely compute-bound, and parallelism is the fix because calibration decomposes into thousands of independent model runs.
42: 
43: - **(c) Large-sample studies.** CAMELS provides 671 US catchments (Addor et al. 2017, https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/21/5293/2017/hess-21-5293-2017.html), each independently calibratable — the definition of an embarrassingly parallel workload in which GPU/cloud throughput directly determines how many catchments can be afforded a *proper* Bayesian treatment rather than point optimization.
44: 
45: ### 3.4 What compute cannot buy
46: 
47: Three hard limits are not computable away:
48: 
49: 1. **Structural error and input (rainfall) uncertainty.** The model is wrong and the rainfall is mismeasured. Renard et al. (2010) report that "poor identifiability may arise when the inference scheme represents rainfall and structural errors using separate probabilistic models," and emphasize "the inherent limitations of inferring inaccurate hydrologic models using rainfall-runoff data with large unknown errors" (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2009WR008328). Explicitly accounting for precipitation error "significantly alters the posterior distribution" of the watershed parameters (Vrugt et al. 2008, https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/treatment-of-input-uncertainty-in-hydrologic-modeling-doing-hydro). These are modeling/likelihood changes (e.g., the Bayesian total error analysis of Kavetski, Kuczera & Franks 2006, https://doi.org/10.1029/2005WR004368), not FLOPs changes.
50: 
51: 2. **Intrinsic autocorrelation of a single chain.** τ is a property of target and sampler. Better samplers reduce it — adaptive Metropolis for correlated parameters (Marshall et al. 2004, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2003WR002378), differential evolution (Vrugt et al. 2009), and gradient-based Hamiltonian Monte Carlo enabled by automatic differentiation of GR4J (Krapu et al. 2022, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2021WR031377). These are the actual levers on "long chains"; hardware is not one of them.
52: 
53: 3. **Data quantity/quality.** No sampler recovers parameters the record cannot identify (Beven & Binley 1992, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305; Renard et al. 2010, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2009WR008328).
54: 
55: ## 4. Synthesis
56: 
57: For the canonical problem that generates "long MCMC chains" — Bayesian calibration of a lumped conceptual model on one catchment — the binding constraint is statistical (posterior geometry, equifinality, autocorrelation, structural/input error), while the per-iteration cost is negligible. GPUs change throughput, not τ; the efficient fix is a better sampler, a reparameterization, a better integrator, or an explicit error model. So the headline answer is NOT COMPUTE-BOUND. But at two real levels — expensive distributed/high-dimensional models, and large-sample multi-catchment studies — compute is a genuine, currently-binding blocker, and there the workload is embarrassingly parallel across parameter sets, chains, and catchments, so massive GPU/cloud parallelism directly changes what can be attempted and concluded. Those are captured below as compute signals, not as the primary limiter of the "long chains" question.
58: 
59: VERDICT: NOT COMPUTE-BOUND

(End of file - total 59 lines)
</content>

# Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching

Paul G. Constantine Affiliation: Applied Mathematics and Statistics  
Colorado School of Mines  
Golden, Colorado 80401  
Email: pconstan@mines.edu    Armin Eftekhari and Michael B. Wakin Affiliation: Electrical Engineering and Computer Science  
Colorado School of Mines  
Golden, Colorado 80401  
Email: aeftekha,mwakin@mines.edu

###### Abstract

Active subspaces are an emerging set of tools for identifying and exploiting the most important directions in the space of a computer simulation’s input parameters; these directions depend on the simulation’s quantity of interest, which we treat as a function from inputs to outputs. To identify a function’s active subspace, one must compute the eigenpairs of a matrix derived from the function’s gradient, which presents challenges when the gradient is not available as a subroutine. We numerically study two methods for estimating the necessary eigenpairs using only linear measurements of the function’s gradient. In practice, these measurements can be estimated by finite differences using only two function evaluations, regardless of the dimension of the function’s input space.

## I Active subspaces

Modern physics and engineering simulations take several inputs—e.g., boundary conditions, material properties, and forcings—and output several quantities of interests. The scientist uses these simulations to study the relationship between inputs and outputs. Uncertainty quantification seeks precise characterization of the simulation’s quantities of interest subject to variability in the inputs. These characterizations often reduce to parameter studies—such as optimization, integration, or response surface modeling—that treat the simulation as a mapping between inputs 𝐱\\mathbf{x} and a quantity of interest f⁡(𝐱)f(\\mathbf{x}). However, thorough parameter studies quickly become infeasible as the dimension of 𝐱\\mathbf{x} grows, particularly if evaluating f⁡(𝐱)f(\\mathbf{x}) (i.e., running the physical simulation) is computationally expensive. To combat this curse of dimensionality, one may seek a low-dimensional parameterization of f⁡(𝐱)f(\\mathbf{x}) that (i) maintains the input/output representation and (ii) enables otherwise infeasible parameter studies. One idea is to identify the least important input parameters and fix them at nominal values, thus reducing the dimension of the parameter study. Such identification is the domain of *sensitivity analysis*, and several techniques exist that use a few simulation runs to screen the inputs’ importance—such as local perturbations, elementary effects, or sensitivity indices \[[1](#bib.bib1)\]. A more general approach is to identify important linear combinations of the inputs 𝐱\\mathbf{x} and focus parameter studies along the associated directions. *Active subspaces* are defined by important directions in the high-dimensional space of inputs; once identified, the scientist can exploit the active subspace to enable otherwise infeasible parameter studies for expensive simulations \[[2](#bib.bib2)\].

Assume that 𝐱∈ℝm\\mathbf{x}\\in\\mathbb{R}^{m} is a vector of simulation inputs, and let the input space be equipped with a probability density function ρ⁡(𝐱)\\rho(\\mathbf{x}) that is strictly positive in the domain of ff and zero outside the domain. In practice, ρ\\rho identifies the set of inputs of interest and quantifies the variability. We assume that the independent inputs have been shifted and scaled to be centered at the origin and have equal variances. Assume that f:ℝm→ℝf:\\mathbb{R}^{m}\\rightarrow\\mathbb{R} is continuous, square-integrable with respect to ρ\\rho, and differentiable with gradient vector ∇f∈ℝm\\nabla f\\in\\mathbb{R}^{m}; also assume that ff’s gradient is square-integrable with respect to ρ\\rho. The active subspace is defined by the first n<mn<m eigenvectors of the following m×mm\\times m symmetric positive semi-definite matrix,

𝑪\=∫∇f∇fTρd𝐱\=𝑾Λ𝑾T,\\bm{C}\\;=\\;\\int\\nabla f\\,\\nabla f^{T}\\,\\rho\\,d\\mathbf{x}\\;=\\;\\bm{W}\\Lambda\\bm{W}^{T},

(1)

where the non-negative eigenvalues are ordered in descending order. The eigenvalue λi\\lambda\_{i} measures the average change in ff subject to perturbations in 𝐱\\mathbf{x} along the corresponding eigenvector 𝐰i\\mathbf{w}\_{i},

λi\=∫(∇fT𝐰i)2ρd𝐱.\\lambda\_{i}\\;=\\;\\int(\\nabla f^{T}\\mathbf{w}\_{i})^{2}\\,\\rho\\,d\\mathbf{x}.

(2)

For example, if λi\=0\\lambda\_{i}=0, then ff is constant along the direction 𝐰i\\mathbf{w}\_{i}. If ff is constant along a direction, then one can ignore this direction when studying the behavior of ff under changes in 𝐱\\mathbf{x}. Suppose that the first n<mn<m eigenvalues are much larger than the trailing m−nm-n, and let 𝑾1\\bm{W}\_{1} be the first nn columns of the orthogonal eigenvector matrix 𝑾\\bm{W}. Then a reasonable approximation for ff is

f⁡(𝐱)≈g⁡(𝑾1T​𝐱),f(\\mathbf{x})\\;\\approx\\;g(\\bm{W}\_{1}^{T}\\mathbf{x}),

(3)

where gg is a properly constructed map from ℝn\\mathbb{R}^{n} to ℝ\\mathbb{R}. In \[[3](#bib.bib3)\], we study a particular construction of gg, its approximation properties, and how those properties change when 𝑾1\\bm{W}\_{1} is estimated.

There are several recent works that study models similar to ([3](#S1.E3 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) in uncertainty quantification \[[4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5)\], computational engineering \[[6](#bib.bib6), [7](#bib.bib7), [8](#bib.bib8), [9](#bib.bib9)\], and approximation theory \[[10](#bib.bib10), [11](#bib.bib11)\]. In statistics, subspace-based dimension reduction has wide use in regression modeling under the monikers *sufficient dimension reduction* \[[12](#bib.bib12)\] and *efficient dimension reduction* \[[13](#bib.bib13)\]. Many in that community have recognized the connection between the dimension reduction space and the matrix 𝑪\\bm{C} in ([1](#S1.E1 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")); see \[[14](#bib.bib14), [15](#bib.bib15)\]. However, in contrast to our case where the gradient ∇f\\nabla f is given, the gradient of the regression function with respect to predictors must be learned. Additionally, there is no random noise in computer simulations in contrast to regression modeling.

The tremendous potential benefits of dimension reduction drive us to pursue methods to estimate the eigenvalues Λ\\Lambda and eigenvectors 𝑾\\bm{W} from ([1](#S1.E1 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")). In \[[16](#bib.bib16)\], we analyze the following Monte Carlo method. First, draw MM samples {𝐱i}\\{\\mathbf{x}\_{i}\\} independently according to ρ\\rho. For each 𝐱i\\mathbf{x}\_{i}, compute ∇fi\=∇f​(𝐱i)\\nabla f\_{i}=\\nabla f(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}). Then compute

𝑪≈𝑪^\=1M∑i\=1M∇fi∇fiT\=𝑾^Λ^𝑾^T.\\bm{C}\\;\\approx\\;\\widehat{\\bm{C}}\\;=\\;\\frac{1}{M}\\sum\_{i=1}^{M}\\nabla f\_{i}\\,\\nabla f\_{i}^{T}\\;=\\;\\widehat{\\bm{W}}\\widehat{\\Lambda}\\widehat{\\bm{W}}^{T}.

(4)

In \[[16](#bib.bib16)\], we use tools from nonasymptotic random matrix theory to study the approximation error in the estimated eigenvalues and subspaces \[[17](#bib.bib17), [18](#bib.bib18)\]. The approach assumes that one has access to the gradient ∇f​(𝐱)\\nabla f(\\mathbf{x}) as a black box, which is not unreasonable in modern simulation codes due to adjoint methods or algorithmic differentiation \[[19](#bib.bib19)\]. However, many legacy simulation codes lack gradient routines, and one must estimate the eigenpairs with only evaluations of f⁡(𝐱)f(\\mathbf{x}).

## II Estimating active subspaces without gradients

When the gradient is not available as a black box, one might estimate the gradient through evaluations of ff, e.g., with finite differences or related techniques \[[20](#bib.bib20)\]. A first-order finite difference approximation to the gradient vector requires m+1m+1 evaluations of ff, so estimating 𝑪^\\widehat{\\bm{C}} in ([4](#S1.E4 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) takes M⁡(m+1)M(m+1) evaluations, which may be prohibitively expensive for large-scale simulations. To surmount this challenge, we take advantage of a finite difference approximation of directional derivatives. For sufficiently small h\>0h>0 and 𝐚∈ℝm\\mathbf{a}\\in\\mathbb{R}^{m},

∇f(𝐱)T𝐚≈(f(𝐱+h𝐚)−f(𝐱))/h.\\nabla f(\\mathbf{x})^{T}\\mathbf{a}\\;\\approx\\;(f(\\mathbf{x}+h\\mathbf{a})-f(\\mathbf{x}))/h.

(5)

The left side of ([5](#S2.E5 "In II Estimating active subspaces without gradients ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) can be interpreted as a linear measurement of the gradient vector, and the right side takes only two evaluations of ff—regardless of the dimension mm. We study two techniques that exploit ([5](#S2.E5 "In II Estimating active subspaces without gradients ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) to estimate 𝑾1\\bm{W}\_{1} from ([1](#S1.E1 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) using only evaluations of ff. The relationship ([5](#S2.E5 "In II Estimating active subspaces without gradients ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) is also exploited in the works \[[10](#bib.bib10), [11](#bib.bib11)\] to reconstruct functions of the form f⁡(𝐱)\=g⁡(𝑨​𝐱)f(\\mathbf{x})=g(\\bm{A}\\mathbf{x}), where 𝑨∈ℝn×m\\bm{A}\\in\\mathbb{R}^{n\\times m}. Note the subtle difference between this reconstruction and the approximation model in ([3](#S1.E3 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")). Our goal in this paper is to estimate 𝑾1\\bm{W}\_{1}, not propose a choice for gg in ([3](#S1.E3 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")). Another important difference is in the linear measurement operator; \[[10](#bib.bib10), [11](#bib.bib11)\] use the same operator for each ∇fi\\nabla f\_{i} in ([4](#S1.E4 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")), while we use an independent measurement operator for each ∇fi\\nabla f\_{i}.

### II-A Eigenvectors from projections

Our first approach is based on work by Qi and Hughes \[[21](#bib.bib21)\] for estimating principal components from linear measurements of a collection of vectors. Suppose that 𝐳i∈ℝm\\mathbf{z}\_{i}\\in\\mathbb{R}^{m}, i\=1,…,Mi=1,\\dots,M, are independent, zero-mean random vectors of the form

𝐳i\=∑j\=1dwi​j​σj​𝐯j,wi​j∼𝒩⁡(0,1),\\mathbf{z}\_{i}\\;=\\;\\sum\_{j=1}^{d}w\_{ij}\\,\\sigma\_{j}\\,\\mathbf{v}\_{j},\\qquad w\_{ij}\\sim\\mathcal{N}(0,1),

(6)

where the 𝐯j\\mathbf{v}\_{j} are orthonormal vectors. Let 𝑬i∈ℝm×k\\bm{E}\_{i}\\in\\mathbb{R}^{m\\times k}, k<mk<m, have independent standard Gaussian entries, and define the measurements 𝐦i\=𝑬iT​𝐳i\\mathbf{m}\_{i}\\;=\\;\\bm{E}\_{i}^{T}\\mathbf{z}\_{i}. Then the orthogonal projection of 𝐳i\\mathbf{z}\_{i} onto the column space of 𝑬i\\bm{E}\_{i} is

𝒫i​𝐳i:=𝑬i​(𝑬iT​𝑬i)−1​𝐦i\=𝑬i​(𝑬iT​𝑬i)−1​𝑬iT​𝐳i.\\mathcal{P}\_{i}\\mathbf{z}\_{i}\\;:=\\;\\bm{E}\_{i}(\\bm{E}\_{i}^{T}\\bm{E}\_{i})^{-1}\\mathbf{m}\_{i}\\;=\\;\\bm{E}\_{i}(\\bm{E}\_{i}^{T}\\bm{E}\_{i})^{-1}\\bm{E}\_{i}^{T}\\mathbf{z}\_{i}.

(8)

converge to the vectors 𝐯1,…,𝐯d\\mathbf{v}\_{1},\\dots,\\mathbf{v}\_{d} as MM goes to infinity. The eigenvalues converge to quantities related to σi\\sigma\_{i} from ([6](#S2.E6 "In II-A Eigenvectors from projections ‣ II Estimating active subspaces without gradients ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")). In fact, their results show how to estimate the mean and principal components even when the model ([6](#S2.E6 "In II-A Eigenvectors from projections ‣ II Estimating active subspaces without gradients ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) has a nonzero mean and random noise.

There is no reason to suspect that the gradient vectors ∇fi\\nabla f\_{i} from ([4](#S1.E4 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) satisfy the model ([6](#S2.E6 "In II-A Eigenvectors from projections ‣ II Estimating active subspaces without gradients ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")). Nonetheless, we can numerically check if the eigenvectors of the matrix

𝑪^𝒫\=1M∑i\=1M𝒫i∇fi(𝒫i∇fi)T,\\widehat{\\bm{C}}\_{\\mathcal{P}}\\;=\\;\\frac{1}{M}\\sum\_{i=1}^{M}\\mathcal{P}\_{i}\\nabla f\_{i}\\,(\\mathcal{P}\_{i}\\nabla f\_{i})^{T},

(9)

where 𝒫i\\mathcal{P}\_{i} is defined as in ([7](#S2.E7 "In II-A Eigenvectors from projections ‣ II Estimating active subspaces without gradients ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")), are close to the eigenvectors of ([4](#S1.E4 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) for chosen test problems. If so, we can exploit the finite difference relationship ([5](#S2.E5 "In II Estimating active subspaces without gradients ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) to efficiently estimate each element of the kk\-vector 𝑬iT∇fi\\bm{E}\_{i}^{T}\\nabla f\_{i}, which is the analogue of 𝐦i\\mathbf{m}\_{i} in ([7](#S2.E7 "In II-A Eigenvectors from projections ‣ II Estimating active subspaces without gradients ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")). In this case, we can estimate the eigenvectors 𝑾^\\widehat{\\bm{W}} from ([4](#S1.E4 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) using M⁡(k+1)<M⁡(m+1)M(k+1)<M(m+1) evaluations of ff. Note that, by the analysis in \[[21](#bib.bib21)\], we do not expect the eigenvalues of 𝑪^𝒫\\widehat{\\bm{C}}\_{\\mathcal{P}} to converge to those of 𝑪^\\widehat{\\bm{C}}.

### II-B Low-rank approximation from linear measurements

Our second approach is based on low-rank approximation of the matrix of gradients 𝑮^\=\[∇f1,…,∇fM\]∈ℝm×M\\widehat{\\bm{G}}=\[\\nabla f\_{1},\\dots,\\nabla f\_{M}\]\\in\\mathbb{R}^{m\\times M} using linear measurements of the gradients. Define the linear measurement operator ℳ⁡(⋅)\\mathcal{M}(\\cdot) as

ℳ⁡(𝑮^):=\[𝑬1T∇f1⋯𝑬MT∇fM\],\\mathcal{M}(\\widehat{\\bm{G}})\\;:=\\;\\begin{bmatrix}\\bm{E}\_{1}^{T}\\nabla f\_{1}&\\cdots&\\bm{E}\_{M}^{T}\\nabla f\_{M}\\end{bmatrix},

(10)

where 𝑬i∈ℝm×k\\bm{E}\_{i}\\in\\mathbb{R}^{m\\times k} has independent standard Gaussian entries as in the previous section. Let rr be the rank of the low-rank approximation. We seek matrices 𝑨∈ℝm×r\\bm{A}\\in\\mathbb{R}^{m\\times r} and 𝑩∈ℝM×r\\bm{B}\\in\\mathbb{R}^{M\\times r} that solve

minimize𝑨,𝑩​‖ℳ⁡(𝑮^)−ℳ⁡(𝑨​𝑩T)‖F,\\underset{\\bm{A},\\,\\bm{B}}{\\operatorname{minimize}}\\;\\|\\mathcal{M}(\\widehat{\\bm{G}})-\\mathcal{M}(\\bm{A}\\bm{B}^{T})\\|\_{F},

(11)

where ∥⋅∥F\\|\\cdot\\|\_{F} is the Frobenius norm. We estimate the minimizers with alternating least-squares. Given 𝑨\\bm{A}, ([11](#S2.E11 "In II-B Low-rank approximation from linear measurements ‣ II Estimating active subspaces without gradients ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) is a linear least-squares problem for 𝑩\\bm{B}. Similarly, given 𝑩\\bm{B}, ([11](#S2.E11 "In II-B Low-rank approximation from linear measurements ‣ II Estimating active subspaces without gradients ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) is a linear least-squares problem for 𝑨\\bm{A}. We choose a starting value for 𝑨\\bm{A} as the first rr eigenvectors, scaled by the square-roots of the first rr eigenvalues, of 𝑪^𝒫\\widehat{\\bm{C}}\_{\\mathcal{P}} in ([9](#S2.E9 "In II-A Eigenvectors from projections ‣ II Estimating active subspaces without gradients ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")). In this sense, the alternating least-squares can be considered an iterative refinement on the estimates from the first method. Once 𝑨\\bm{A} and 𝑩\\bm{B} are estimated, we compute the left singular vectors of 𝑨​𝑩T\\bm{A}\\bm{B}^{T} to estimate 𝑾1\\bm{W}\_{1} in ([3](#S1.E3 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")).

The low-rank model 𝑨​𝑩T\\bm{A}\\bm{B}^{T} requires the user to choose the rank rr. To solve the least-squares subproblem for 𝑨\\bm{A} without additional regularization, we need rr less than the number kk of linear measurements (i.e., the number of columns in 𝑬i\\bm{E}\_{i}). Additionally, we are guided by the ultimate goal of the dimension reduction, which is to construct gg in ([3](#S1.E3 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")). Without prior knowledge of the relationship between ff and 𝐱\\mathbf{x}, constructing a response surface is generally too expensive in more than a handful of dimensions. Thus, we may reasonably keep rr less than 8 or 9. If there is no gap within the first 8 or 9 eigenvalue estimates, then ([3](#S1.E3 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) may be inappropriate.

## III Experiments

We test the two methods on two functions: (i) a quadratic polynomial in m\=10m=10 dimensions and (ii) a quantity of interest from the solution of a PDE whose operator coefficients depend on m\=100m=100 variables. In each experiment, we compute 𝑪^\\widehat{\\bm{C}} from ([4](#S1.E4 "In I Active subspaces ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")) with a fixed number MM of gradient samples, and we consider the eigenpairs 𝑾^\\widehat{\\bm{W}} and Λ^\\widehat{\\Lambda} to be the *true* values. We compute the error in the first six eigenvalue estimates and the error in the subspaces defined by the eigenvectors estimates as

respectively, where λ~i\\tilde{\\lambda}\_{i} and 𝑾~\\tilde{\\bm{W}} are the eigenvalue and eigenvector estimates, respectively, from the linear measurement-based approaches. The subscript 1 on the matrices 𝑾^\\widehat{\\bm{W}} and 𝑾~\\tilde{\\bm{W}} indicates that they contain only the first nn columns; we note nn when needed. We do not expect the eigenvalue estimates from the projection-based method in Section [II-A](#S2.SS1 "II-A Eigenvectors from projections ‣ II Estimating active subspaces without gradients ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching") to converge, but we report them to compare with the errors from the alternating least-squares approach. We do not study the approximation properties of the finite differences in ([5](#S2.E5 "In II Estimating active subspaces without gradients ‣ Computing Active Subspaces Efficiently with Gradient Sketching")), e.g., by varying the finite difference parameter hh. ## IV Conclusion

We have studied the approximation properties of two methods for estimating the eigenvectors and eigenvalues that define a multivariate function’s active subspace. These methods use linear measurements of the gradient instead of the full gradient, which can be efficiently computed with finite differences. The first method, based on work by Qi and Hughes \[[21](#bib.bib21)\], uses random projections of the gradient. The second uses a low-rank approximation of the matrix of gradient measurements fit with an alternating least-squares method. The low-rank approximation performs better than the projection-based method in two numerical tests. Future work will (i) analyze the improvement with the low-rank approximation and (ii) study the effect of finite difference approximations of the linear measurements. These initial results are sufficiently promising to pursue such studies.

# ACCELERATING MCMC WITH ACTIVE SUBSPACES
Paul G. Constantine
††thanks: Ben L.˜Fryrear Assistant Professor, Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO 80401 (paul.constantine@mines.edu).

###### Abstract
The Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method is the computational workhorse for Bayesian inverse problems. However, MCMC struggles in high-dimensional parameter spaces, since its iterates must sequentially explore the high-dimensional space. This struggle is compounded in physical applications when the nonlinear forward model is computationally expensive. One approach to accelerate MCMC is to reduce the dimension of the state space. *Active subspaces* are part of an emerging set of tools for subspace-based dimension reduction. An active subspace in a given inverse problem indicates a separation between a low-dimensional subspace that is informed by the data and its orthogonal complement that is constrained by the prior. With this information, one can run the sequential MCMC on the active variables while sampling independently according to the prior on the inactive variables. However, this approach to increase efficiency may introduce bias. We provide a bound on the Hellinger distance between the true posterior and its active subspace-exploiting approximation. And we demonstrate the active subspace-accelerated MCMC on two computational examples: (i) a two-dimensional parameter space with a quadratic forward model and one-dimensional active subspace and (ii) a 100-dimensional parameter space with a PDE-based forward model and a two-dimensional active subspace.
###### keywords
MCMC, active subspaces, dimension reduction
###### AMS

## 1 Introduction
Modern computing enables powerful Bayesian inference methods to quantify uncertainty in complex science and engineering models. The workhorse of these methods is Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which constructs a Markov chain whose steps produce correlated samples from the conditional posterior density of the parameters given data. Several excellent references introduce and develop the theory and practice of MCMC in the context of statistical inverse problems [3, 22, 27]. However, standard MCMC remains an inefficient tool when (i) the dimension of the parameter space is large and/or (ii) the forward model in the likelihood is expensive. Recent papers have proposed strategies to increase MCMC’s efficiency by introducing structure-exploiting proposal densities [1, 20, 28, 18, 24, 5]. When the forward model numerically approximates a PDE solution, the differential operators may enable MCMC variants whose state space dimension is independent of the PDE discretization [4, 5, 24, 14].
MCMC struggles in high dimensions because the Markov chain must explore the high-dimensional space to find regions of relatively high posterior probability. The recent paper by Cui, et al. [14] seeks to reduce the Markov chain’s state space dimension by identifying a low-dimensional *likelihood-informed subspace*. When an inverse problem is ill-posed, the data does not inform all parameters; Cui, et al. use the eigendecomposition of the negative log-likelihood’s Hessian—averaged over the parameter space with respect to the posterior—to identify a data-informed subspace; its orthogonal complement is informed by the prior. This separation leads to an efficient MCMC method when the forward model is twice differentiable, the prior is Gaussian, and the noise is Gaussian. They have extended these ideas to develop optimal posterior covariance approximations for linear forward models [26] and dimension-independent methods for infinite dimensional problems [13].
Our recent work in *active subspaces* resembles the subspace-based dimension reduction of Cui, et al. [14], though the context is broader than statistical inverse problems. The active subspace is defined for a scalar-valued, multivariate function; the active subspace basis consists of the principal eigenvectors of the average outer product of the gradient with itself. When a function admits an active subspace, one can exploit the low-dimensional structure to enable approximation, integration, and optimization in high dimensions [9, 11, 8]. We have applied this technique to help study aerospace models [10, 23], hydrological models [21], and solar cell models [12]. We review active subspaces and the resulting approximations in section 2.
In this paper, we seek to discover the active subspace from the negative log-likelihood in a Bayesian inverse problem. If the negative log-likelihood admits an active subspace, then we use the active subspace to construct a function that approximates the Bayesian posterior. The approximate posterior enables an efficient MCMC that exploits the low-dimensional structure; the Markov chain operates on the active variables (i.e., the coordinates of the active subspace), while the inactive variables are drawn independently from their derived prior. In contrast to the likelihood-informed subspace of Cui, et al. [14], the active subspace is defined by the gradient of the negative log-likelihood instead of a Gauss-Newton-based approximation of its Hessian. Additionally, the matrix that defines the active subspace is an average with respect to the prior as opposed to the posterior. This choice is computationally appealing, since one can draw independent samples from the prior and estimate integrals with standard Monte Carlo. Consequently, computing the active subspace is a preprocessing step that occurs before the MCMC.
In section 3, we analyze the approximation error in the posterior, measured by the Hellinger distance. We detail the MCMC algorithm with the active subspace in section 4. We demonstrate the approach in two synthetic Bayesian inverse problems: (i) a quadratic forward model with a two-dimensional parameter space and (ii) a forward model governed by Poisson’s equation, where the data are the PDE solution—perturbed by noise—at points on the boundary, and the parameters are the coefficients of the differential operator. We describe the models and show results in section 5. In section 6, we summarize the method and discuss some practical limitations and future work.

# ACCELERATING MCMC WITH ACTIVE SUBSPACES

Paul G. Constantine ††thanks: Ben L.˜Fryrear Assistant Professor, Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO 80401 (paul.constantine@mines.edu).    Carson Kent ††thanks: Ph.D. student, Institute for Computational and Mathematical Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305 (crkent@stanford.edu).    Tan Bui-Thanh ††thanks: Assistant Professor, Department of Aerospace Engineering and Engineering Mechanics, Institute for Computational Engineering and Sciences, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX 78705 (tanbui@ices.utexas.edu).

###### Abstract

The Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method is the computational workhorse for Bayesian inverse problems. However, MCMC struggles in high-dimensional parameter spaces, since its iterates must sequentially explore the high-dimensional space. This struggle is compounded in physical applications when the nonlinear forward model is computationally expensive. One approach to accelerate MCMC is to reduce the dimension of the state space. *Active subspaces* are part of an emerging set of tools for subspace-based dimension reduction. An active subspace in a given inverse problem indicates a separation between a low-dimensional subspace that is informed by the data and its orthogonal complement that is constrained by the prior. With this information, one can run the sequential MCMC on the active variables while sampling independently according to the prior on the inactive variables. However, this approach to increase efficiency may introduce bias. We provide a bound on the Hellinger distance between the true posterior and its active subspace-exploiting approximation. And we demonstrate the active subspace-accelerated MCMC on two computational examples: (i) a two-dimensional parameter space with a quadratic forward model and one-dimensional active subspace and (ii) a 100-dimensional parameter space with a PDE-based forward model and a two-dimensional active subspace.

###### keywords

MCMC, active subspaces, dimension reduction

###### AMS

65C40, 65D15

## 1 Introduction

Modern computing enables powerful Bayesian inference methods to quantify uncertainty in complex science and engineering models. The workhorse of these methods is Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which constructs a Markov chain whose steps produce correlated samples from the conditional posterior density of the parameters given data. Several excellent references introduce and develop the theory and practice of MCMC in the context of statistical inverse problems \[[3](#bib.bib3), [22](#bib.bib22), [27](#bib.bib27)\]. However, standard MCMC remains an inefficient tool when (i) the dimension of the parameter space is large and/or (ii) the forward model in the likelihood is expensive. Recent papers have proposed strategies to increase MCMC’s efficiency by introducing structure-exploiting proposal densities \[[1](#bib.bib1), [20](#bib.bib20), [28](#bib.bib28), [18](#bib.bib18), [24](#bib.bib24), [5](#bib.bib5)\]. When the forward model numerically approximates a PDE solution, the differential operators may enable MCMC variants whose state space dimension is independent of the PDE discretization \[[4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5), [24](#bib.bib24), [14](#bib.bib14)\].

MCMC struggles in high dimensions because the Markov chain must explore the high-dimensional space to find regions of relatively high posterior probability. The recent paper by Cui, et al. \[[14](#bib.bib14)\] seeks to reduce the Markov chain’s state space dimension by identifying a low-dimensional *likelihood-informed subspace*. When an inverse problem is ill-posed, the data does not inform all parameters; Cui, et al. use the eigendecomposition of the negative log-likelihood’s Hessian—averaged over the parameter space with respect to the posterior—to identify a data-informed subspace; its orthogonal complement is informed by the prior. This separation leads to an efficient MCMC method when the forward model is twice differentiable, the prior is Gaussian, and the noise is Gaussian. They have extended these ideas to develop optimal posterior covariance approximations for linear forward models \[[26](#bib.bib26)\] and dimension-independent methods for infinite dimensional problems \[[13](#bib.bib13)\].

Our recent work in *active subspaces* resembles the subspace-based dimension reduction of Cui, et al. \[[14](#bib.bib14)\], though the context is broader than statistical inverse problems. The active subspace is defined for a scalar-valued, multivariate function; the active subspace basis consists of the principal eigenvectors of the average outer product of the gradient with itself. When a function admits an active subspace, one can exploit the low-dimensional structure to enable approximation, integration, and optimization in high dimensions \[[9](#bib.bib9), [11](#bib.bib11), [8](#bib.bib8)\]. We have applied this technique to help study aerospace models \[[10](#bib.bib10), [23](#bib.bib23)\], hydrological models \[[21](#bib.bib21)\], and solar cell models \[[12](#bib.bib12)\]. We review active subspaces and the resulting approximations in section [2](#S2 "2 Active subspaces ‣ ACCELERATING MCMC WITH ACTIVE SUBSPACES").

In this paper, we seek to discover the active subspace from the negative log-likelihood in a Bayesian inverse problem. If the negative log-likelihood admits an active subspace, then we use the active subspace to construct a function that approximates the Bayesian posterior. The approximate posterior enables an efficient MCMC that exploits the low-dimensional structure; the Markov chain operates on the active variables (i.e., the coordinates of the active subspace), while the inactive variables are drawn independently from their derived prior. In contrast to the likelihood-informed subspace of Cui, et al. \[[14](#bib.bib14)\], the active subspace is defined by the gradient of the negative log-likelihood instead of a Gauss-Newton-based approximation of its Hessian. Additionally, the matrix that defines the active subspace is an average with respect to the prior as opposed to the posterior. This choice is computationally appealing, since one can draw independent samples from the prior and estimate integrals with standard Monte Carlo. Consequently, computing the active subspace is a preprocessing step that occurs before the MCMC.

In section [3](#S3 "3 Approximating the Bayesian posterior ‣ ACCELERATING MCMC WITH ACTIVE SUBSPACES"), we analyze the approximation error in the posterior, measured by the Hellinger distance. We detail the MCMC algorithm with the active subspace in section [4](#S4 "4 MCMC with the active subspace ‣ ACCELERATING MCMC WITH ACTIVE SUBSPACES"). We demonstrate the approach in two synthetic Bayesian inverse problems: (i) a quadratic forward model with a two-dimensional parameter space and (ii) a forward model governed by Poisson’s equation, where the data are the PDE solution—perturbed by noise—at points on the boundary, and the parameters are the coefficients of the differential operator. We describe the models and show results in section [5](#S5 "5 Numerical experiments ‣ ACCELERATING MCMC WITH ACTIVE SUBSPACES"). In section [6](#S6 "6 Summary and conclusions ‣ ACCELERATING MCMC WITH ACTIVE SUBSPACES"), we summarize the method and discuss some practical limitations and future work.

### 3.1 Identifying the active subspace

To apply the active subspace machinery from section [2](#S2 "2 Active subspaces ‣ ACCELERATING MCMC WITH ACTIVE SUBSPACES"), we must identify the scalar-valued function f⁡(𝐱)f(\\mathbf{x}) and the density function ρ⁡(𝐱)\\rho(\\mathbf{x}) in ([2](#S2.E2 "In 2 Active subspaces ‣ ACCELERATING MCMC WITH ACTIVE SUBSPACES")). Similar to the likelihood-informed subspace of Cui, et al. \[[14](#bib.bib14)\], we choose f⁡(𝐱)f(\\mathbf{x}) to be the negative log-likelihood,

f⁡(𝐱)\=12​σ2​‖𝐝−𝐦⁡(𝐱)‖2.f(\\mathbf{x})\\;=\\;\\frac{1}{2\\sigma^{2}}\\,\\|\\mathbf{d}-\\mathbf{m}(\\mathbf{x})\\|^{2}.

(21)

This function is often called the *data misfit* function, or just *misfit*, and it is closely related to an optimizer’s objective function in deterministic inverse problems. For a given point in the parameter space, f⁡(𝐱)f(\\mathbf{x}) measures how far the modeled observations are from the given data. If we use the misfit to define the active subspace, then the orthogonal complement—i.e., the inactive subspace—identifies directions along which the likelihood is relatively flat. Perturbing the parameters along the inactive subspace changes the likelihood relatively little, on average. We wish to exploit this structure, when present, to accelerate the MCMC. The gradient of the misfit is

∇f(𝐱)\=1σ2∇𝐦(𝐱)T(𝐝−𝐦(𝐱)),\\nabla f(\\mathbf{x})\\;=\\;\\frac{1}{\\sigma^{2}}\\,\\nabla\\mathbf{m}(\\mathbf{x})^{T}\\,(\\mathbf{d}-\\mathbf{m}(\\mathbf{x})),

(22)

where ∇𝐦∈ℝd×m\\nabla\\mathbf{m}\\in\\mathbb{R}^{d\\times m} is the Jacobian of the parameter-to-observable map. The misfit and its gradient depend on the data 𝐝\\mathbf{d}; this becomes important when we choose ρ\\rho.

Cui, et al. \[[14](#bib.bib14)\] average the misfit’s prior-preconditioned Gauss-Newton Hessian with respect to the posterior density in ([20](#S3.E20 "In 3 Approximating the Bayesian posterior ‣ ACCELERATING MCMC WITH ACTIVE SUBSPACES")) to estimate the likelihood-informed subspace.   Line 177: One of the most critical considerations when selecting a force-field for long-chain molecules is whether to employ an all-atom or a united-atom variant. In all-atom (or explicit hydrogen) force-fields, every atom in the molecule is explicitly treated and parameterized. On the contrary, united-atom force-fields do not explicitly treat non-polar hydrogen atoms, but rather group them with carbon atoms and assign parameters to the resultant CH, CH2, or CH3 ‘pseudo-atoms’. United-atom force-fields significantly reduce the number of atoms for which non-bonded interactions need to be calculated, thus decreasing the computational expense by up to an order of magnitude \[[11](#B11-materials-09-00651)\]. This has made them very popular in tribology \[[1](#B1-materials-09-00651),[2](#B2-materials-09-00651),[3](#B3-materials-09-00651),[4](#B4-materials-09-00651),[5](#B5-materials-09-00651),[6](#B6-materials-09-00651),[7](#B7-materials-09-00651)\] where the simulation of large, multicomponent systems is often required.

Probably the most significant liquid properties in the simulation of tribological systems are the density and viscosity, since they are inherently linked to the lubricant hydrodynamics. In an MD force-field, the liquid density is mainly governed by the non-bonded (Lennard-Jones and Coulombic) interactions, whilst the viscosity is also heavily influenced by the ‘stiffness’ of the torsional potential \[[12](#B12-materials-09-00651),[13](#B13-materials-09-00651)\]. Previous studies have compared all-atom and united-atom force-field performance in terms of their density and viscosity prediction of long-chain alkanes \[[13](#B13-materials-09-00651),[14](#B14-materials-09-00651),[15](#B15-materials-09-00651)\]; however, they have been limited to only a few variants, and have not included recent parameterizations specifically designed for long-chain molecules \[[16](#B16-materials-09-00651),[17](#B17-materials-09-00651)\]. These previous comparisons have shown that united-atom force-fields consistently under-predict the viscosity of long-chain linear alkanes, with the prediction accuracy deteriorating when longer chain molecules or high pressures are used \[[13](#B13-materials-09-00651),[14](#B14-materials-09-00651),[15](#B15-materials-09-00651)\]. For example, under ambient conditions, united-atom force-fields have been shown to provide a reasonable prediction for the viscosity of C10 (−20%); however, prediction accuracy decreases considerably for longer C16 molecules (−50%) \[[15](#B15-materials-09-00651)\]. Built upon Lean FRO’s LeanREPL ([Lean FRO, 2023](#bib.bibx11)), the Numina Lean Server employs an LRU-based caching mechanism that reuses preloaded environments based on import headers, significantly reducing initialization overhead.   Line 53: The Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method is the computational workhorse for Bayesian inverse problems. However, MCMC struggles in high-dimensional parameter spaces, since its iterates must sequentially explore the high-dimensional space. This struggle is compounded in physical applications when the nonlinear forward model is computationally expensive. One approach to accelerate MCMC is to reduce the dimension of the state space. *Active subspaces* are part of an emerging set of tools for subspace-based dimension reduction. An active subspace in a given inverse problem indicates a separation between a low-dimensional subspace that is informed by the data and its orthogonal complement that is constrained by the prior. With this information, one can run the sequential MCMC on the active variables while sampling independently according to the prior on the inactive variables. However, this approach to increase efficiency may introduce bias. We provide a bound on the Hellinger distance between the true posterior and its active subspace-exploiting approximation. And we demonstrate the active subspace-accelerated MCMC on two computational examples: (i) a two-dimensional parameter space with a quadratic forward model and one-dimensional active subspace and (ii) a 100-dimensional parameter space with a PDE-based forward model and a two-dimensional active subspace.

  Line 65: Modern computing enables powerful Bayesian inference methods to quantify uncertainty in complex science and engineering models. The workhorse of these methods is Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which constructs a Markov chain whose steps produce correlated samples from the conditional posterior density of the parameters given data. Several excellent references introduce and develop the theory and practice of MCMC in the context of statistical inverse problems \[[3](#bib.bib3), [22](#bib.bib22), [27](#bib.bib27)\]. However, standard MCMC remains an inefficient tool when (i) the dimension of the parameter space is large and/or (ii) the forward model in the likelihood is expensive. Recent papers have proposed strategies to increase MCMC’s efficiency by introducing structure-exploiting proposal densities \[[1](#bib.bib1), [20](#bib.bib20), [28](#bib.bib28), [18](#bib.bib18), [24](#bib.bib24), [5](#bib.bib5)\]. When the forward model numerically approximates a PDE solution, the differential operators may enable MCMC variants whose state space dimension is independent of the PDE discretization \[[4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5), [24](#bib.bib24), [14](#bib.bib14)\].

  Line 67: MCMC struggles in high dimensions because the Markov chain must explore the high-dimensional space to find regions of relatively high posterior probability. The recent paper by Cui, et al. \[[14](#bib.bib14)\] seeks to reduce the Markov chain’s state space dimension by identifying a low-dimensional *likelihood-informed subspace*. When an inverse problem is ill-posed, the data does not inform all parameters; Cui, et al. use the eigendecomposition of the negative log-likelihood’s Hessian—averaged over the parameter space with respect to the posterior—to identify a data-informed subspace; its orthogonal complement is informed by the prior. This separation leads to an efficient MCMC method when the forward model is twice differentiable, the prior is Gaussian, and the noise is Gaussian. They have extended these ideas to develop optimal posterior covariance approximations for linear forward models \[[26](#bib.bib26)\] and dimension-independent methods for infinite dimensional problems \[[13](#bib.bib13)\].

  Line 71: In this paper, we seek to discover the active subspace from the negative log-likelihood in a Bayesian inverse problem. If the negative log-likelihood admits an active subspace, then we use the active subspace to construct a function that approximates the Bayesian posterior. The approximate posterior enables an efficient MCMC that exploits the low-dimensional structure; the Markov chain operates on the active variables (i.e., the coordinates of the active subspace), while the inactive variables are drawn independently from their derived prior. In contrast to the likelihood-informed subspace of Cui, et al. \[[14](#bib.bib14)\], the active subspace is defined by the gradient of the negative log-likelihood instead of a Gauss-Newton-based approximation of its Hessian. Additionally, the matrix that defines the active subspace is an average with respect to the prior as opposed to the posterior. This choice is computationally appealing, since one can draw independent samples from the prior and estimate integrals with standard Monte Carlo. Consequently, computing the active subspace is a preprocessing step that occurs before the MCMC.

This approach has previously demonstrated success in helping discover new materials in various applications \[[14](#bib.bib14), [15](#bib.bib15), [16](#bib.bib16), [17](#bib.bib17)\]. However, unlike previous approaches, the current work does not constrain substitution by ionic similarity learned from mining materials databases \[[14](#bib.bib14)\] and therefore has a broader search space. We chose 54 elements, indicated by the colored cells in Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Exploring a vast chemical space ‣ 2 Large-scale materials discovery ‣ Accelerating computational materials discovery with artificial intelligence and cloud high-performance computing: from large-scale screening to experimental validation")a, as our starting point for the most likely compositions of Li-conducting solid-state electrolytes. We chose to remove later-row transition metals and most lanthanides because those are not commonly found in Li battery materials. Noble gases and actinides are typically not part of viable functional materials applications and hence were not included. Line 86: Common oxidation states of the 54 elements were obtained from Pymatgen \[[18](#bib.bib18)\] data. To generate the initial structure candidates, we used the 2022 version of the [ICSD](#S5.9) ([ICSD](#S5.9)) \[[19](#bib.bib19)\], and then used Pymatgen \[[18](#bib.bib18)\] StructureMatcher to match similar structures and obtain structure prototypes. We used only the ordered structures with integer site occupancies that quantum mechanical calculations can handle, and performed iso-valent substitutions to those prototypes, which generated 32,598,079 initial candidates. The space groups of those candidates are shown in Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2.1 Exploring a vast chemical space ‣ 2 Large-scale materials discovery ‣ Accelerating computational materials discovery with artificial intelligence and cloud high-performance computing: from large-scale screening to experimental validation")b.
